title: The forgotten strength
hook: cursed to forget his powers until reminded

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sun for breakfast: a baby who leapt for the sun and came home with gifts from every god. Your line was reach anyway. Today, those gifts go missing. Day thirty.

So now you have a child with the strength of the wind, gifts from every god, and no sense of limits at all. What do you think happens? Exactly what you think. Young Hanuman runs wild through the forest hermitages where the sages live. He knocks over their water pots. He tears up their offerings. He scatters their sacred fires. Not cruel, just a kid who doesn't know his own size. And the sages, patient people, reach the end of their patience. They don't take his strength away. They do something stranger. They put a curse on him: he will forget it. He'll have all that power, and not remember he has it, until someone reminds him.
screen: `A CHILD WITH NO LIMITS.` → `THE SAGES' PATIENCE ENDS.` → `HE WILL FORGET.` → `UNTIL SOMEONE REMINDS HIM.`

segments.voice: Years pass. Hanuman grows up gentle, wise, loyal, and he has no idea what he can do. Now jump ahead in the Ramayana. A band of monkeys and bears are standing on the southern shore of India, looking at the ocean. On the far side, somewhere, is the island of Lanka. Someone has to cross it. The text says a hundred yojanas, an enormous distance. One by one, the heroes say how far they could jump. Ten. Twenty. Fifty. Ninety, maybe, but not back. Nobody can do it. And Hanuman sits apart, quiet. He doesn't even volunteer. Then the old bear, Jambavan, walks over to him. And he tells Hanuman his own story. You are the son of the wind. As a baby you leapt for the sun. Every god gave you a gift. Why are you sitting here silent? And as Jambavan speaks, Hanuman remembers. The text says he begins to grow, swelling in size and strength, until the others cheer. Here's what the story knows. The strength was never gone. It was forgotten. That's a very different problem, and most of us have it. We forget what we've already survived, already done, already are. And notice how the curse is lifted. Not by a god. By a friend who remembers you better than you remember yourself. Sometimes that's the most useful thing one person can do for another: tell them their own story back.
screen: `THE OCEAN NOBODY CAN CROSS.` · `HANUMAN SITS APART, QUIET.` · `JAMBAVAN TELLS HIM HIS STORY.` · `FORGOTTEN, NOT GONE.` · then, large: `YOU'RE STRONGER THAN YOU REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a strength you forget you have. Sit and breathe. Be your own Jambavan for two minutes. Remember a hard thing you got through. A time you were braver than you expected. Something you're good at that you stopped counting. Say it to yourself plainly, the way the old bear did: you did this. You are this. Then just sit with it, and let it grow a little. The bell holds the time.
The forgotten strength. Hanuman, cursed to forget his power, until Jambavan reminds him who he is at the edge of the ocean.
Your line: you're stronger than you remember. Today, be someone's Jambavan: remind one person of a strength they've forgotten. Day thirty.

howItsDone: Many Hindus recite the Hanuman Chalisa, a sixteenth-century hymn by Tulsidas, for courage in hard times; it retells his deeds, which devotees describe as a kind of reminding, as Jambavan once reminded him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hero who didn't know he was a hero.
what it means: the strength was forgotten, not gone, and a friend's memory brings it back.
what a scholar hears: the curse is told in the Uttara Kanda; the reminding at the shore is in the Kishkindha Kanda, where Jambavan retells Hanuman's birth.
